questions.question: In user-centered design, how are users involved in developing an application?
options: Users are involved only during requirements analysis.
Users are involved only after the system is deployed.
They are actively or passively involved throughout the overall design lifecycle, including design and implementation.
Users are involved only in final usability testing.
questions.explanation: User-centered design actively or passively involves users in the overall design lifecycle, including design and implementation, with the objective of producing usable software.

questions.question: What is the core design concern for user-centered XR application software?
options: Designing systems that minimize users' involvement in the design lifecycle.
Designing systems that expose the hardware and software internals to laypersons.
Designing systems primarily for expert developers of the XR platform.
Designing usable interactive systems that meet the needs and expectations of laypersons.
questions.explanation: The core concern is designing usable systems that meet the needs and expectations of laypersons, and the XR application software is interactive software intended for laypersons.

questions.question: What is required to obtain usable application software instead of a haphazard or ad hoc manner?
options: Skipping to final coding after the first idea.
Following an unstructured brainstorming process.
Using intuition alone to pick the best valid design.
Following a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle.
questions.explanation: Obtaining usable application software requires following a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle rather than working in a haphazard or ad hoc manner.

questions.question: What does a software development lifecycle comprehensively capture?
options: The design and development activities needed to build the software.
Only the post-deployment marketing plan.
Only the final user manual and help screens.
Only the hardware procurement decisions for the XR system.
questions.explanation: A software development lifecycle is a systematic, structured set of connected stages that comprehensively capture and represent the design and development activities needed to build the software.

questions.question: What can the term software engineering represent when discussing software development?
options: A method for skipping design-prototype-evaluate cycles.
A single unstructured coding phase.
The idea of a software development lifecycle, with software being built in stages.
A specific category of extended reality hardware.
questions.explanation: Software engineering can be used as a single term that represents the idea of a software development lifecycle, and engineering software means building the software in stages.

questions.question: What does the term design space refer to in the arrangement of screen elements?
options: The set of all development stages
The set of all possible designs
The set of all valid user inputs
The set of all functional requirements
questions.explanation: A design space is the set of all possible designs, and the number of arrangements can increase when repetition is allowed.

questions.question: Why does a calendar application have a very large design space?
options: It has a variable and large number of elements to be displayed
It has a fixed and large number of elements to be displayed
It has a fixed and large number of requirements to be gathered
It has a fixed and small number of elements to be displayed
questions.explanation: A calendar application has a fixed and large number of elements to display, such as month names, dates, and possibly the year, so it has a very large design space.

questions.question: What remains true for a calendar application even though many possible designs are invalid?
options: All valid design choices are eliminated by usability rules
A reasonably significant number of valid design choices can remain
Only one valid design choice remains
No valid design choices can remain
questions.explanation: Although dates must be ordered in a particular way, making many designs invalid, a reasonably significant number of valid design choices can remain in most practical systems.

questions.question: Why is a structured software development life cycle useful when choosing among valid designs?
options: It selects a design using developer intuition alone
It removes usability from the design decision
It chooses the design that uses the fewest development stages
It helps identify the best valid design choice in terms of usability
questions.explanation: A systematic software development life cycle helps identify the best valid design choice in terms of usability because intuition may not lead to the single best solution for everyone.

questions.question: In interactive system design, during which stages must users be taken into account?
options: Only the deployment and maintenance stage
All stages of the development lifecycle
Only the design and prototyping stages
Only the requirement-gathering stage
questions.explanation: Users must be taken into account in every stage and involved as active or passive participants.

questions.question: Why does user-centric design of interactive systems require a highly iterative lifecycle?
options: To allow developers to return to earlier stages when user needs change
To proceed only to the next stage without returning to previous stages
To keep the stage sequence fixed after user needs are included
To avoid loops between earlier and later stages
questions.explanation: Including users' needs and expectations changes the stage sequence and creates loops where a developer may return to a previous stage.

questions.question: In an interactive system development lifecycle, what is meant by user feedback in stage iterations?
options: Involving users in different ways, not only through feedback
Involving users only after the system is deployed
Involving users only through feedback
Involving developers in different ways, not only through feedback
questions.explanation: Iterations between stages account for user feedback, which means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.

questions.question: Which part of the iterative interactive system development lifecycle can iterate back to requirement gathering?
options: The feasibility study stage
The code testing stage
The design-prototype-evaluate cycle
The deployment and maintenance stage
questions.explanation: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle has iterations among its stages and also an iteration to the requirement gathering stage.

questions.question: What does the design-prototype-evaluate cycle consist of?
options: Code testing, deployment, and maintenance
Design, prototyping, and early evaluation
Requirement gathering, analysis, and specification
Design, coding, and empirical usability study
questions.explanation: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle consists of design, prototyping, and early evaluation.

questions.question: In the development of interactive systems, who must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards?
options: End users only after the design stage
End users together with the customer or client
Only the customer or client
The client only during the feasibility study
questions.explanation: For interactive systems, end users must be involved from requirement gathering onwards along with the customer or client, whereas typical requirement analysis refers to the client's requirements.

questions.question: Which methods are used for gathering end-user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage?
options: Contextual inquiry, empirical study, and ethnographic studies
Ethnographic studies, code design, and cultural probes
Contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes
Contextual inquiry, code testing, and cultural probes
questions.explanation: The requirement-gathering stage uses methods such as contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes to gather end-user requirements.

questions.question: In the design-prototype-evaluate loop, when can the design be stabilized and the next stage begin?
options: After the empirical study confirms final usability
After code testing confirms the code is bug-free
After evaluation no longer identifies many significantly different problems
After the first prototype has been evaluated
questions.explanation: The design is stabilized and the next stage can begin once iterations have continued until evaluation no longer reveals many significantly different problems.

questions.question: Why should each stage of the design-prototype-evaluate loop be completed quickly?
options: To move directly to code design after a single evaluation
To allow many iterations within a reasonable overall time
To reduce the need for user feedback in every iteration
To allow only one iteration within a reasonable overall time
questions.explanation: The loop and its stages must be completed quickly so that many iterations can occur within a reasonable time; otherwise the overall turnaround time increases significantly.

questions.question: Which design activity is carried out in the design-prototype-evaluate loop?
options: Interface and interaction design from the user's point of view
Empirical study after system deployment
Hardware selection for the final XR system
Code design before the prototype is evaluated
questions.explanation: The loop includes interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view, while code design is a separate later activity.

questions.question: What is the initial sequence for coding and code testing in interactive system development?
options: Coding and implementation, then code testing, then code design
Code testing, then code design, then coding and implementation
Code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing
Code design, then code testing, then coding and implementation
questions.explanation: The traditional sequence is code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

questions.question: Why are fewer iterations between code design, coding, and code testing preferred?
options: Because code design is highly skilled and costly, and late problems are costly to rewrite and test
Because code testing guarantees usability, so fewer design changes are needed
Because code testing is highly skilled and costly, and early designs are easy to change
Because empirical studies are inexpensive, so coding loops are unnecessary
questions.explanation: Fewer iterations are preferred because code design is highly skilled and costly, and late problems are costly to rewrite and test.

questions.question: What are the three evaluation points in the iterative software development life cycle for usable interactive systems?
options: Early evaluation, code testing, and empirical study
Early evaluation, code design, and code testing
Requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study
Code testing, empirical study, and user requirement gathering
questions.explanation: Early evaluation, code testing, and empirical study are the three evaluation points.

questions.question: What does code testing fail to establish?
options: Proper execution of the code
Bug-freeness of the code
Executability of the code
Usability from the end user's point of view
questions.explanation: Code testing ensures the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish usability from the end user's point of view.

questions.question: Why is the empirical study stage a distinguishing feature of interactive system development?
options: Because it only checks that the code is bug-free before release
Because it systematically tests usability with end users, an activity typically absent when end users are not involved
Because it replaces the early evaluation of interface and interaction design
Because it evaluates code executability during coding and implementation
questions.explanation: Empirical study systematically tests usability with end users, and it is typically not part of other software development where end users are not involved.

questions.question: In the iterative design of usable extended reality systems, which loop is intended to be performed quickly?
options: The loop between the design-prototype-evaluate loop and coding, implementation, and empirical studies
The loop between requirement gathering and the design-prototype-evaluate loop
The loop between code design, coding, and code testing
The design-prototype-evaluate loop
questions.explanation: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle is the only loop designed to be performed quickly. The other listed loops should not be frequent.

questions.question: Why should loops other than the design-prototype-evaluate loop be kept infrequent?
options: Because frequent repetition can make code testing sufficient to prove usability
Because frequent repetition can reduce the need to involve end users early
Because frequent repetition can allow more quick design-prototype-evaluate iterations
Because frequent repetition can escalate development cost, delay turnaround, and lead to project abandonment
questions.explanation: Frequent loops other than the design-prototype-evaluate loop can significantly affect project outcome and turnaround time. They can also escalate development cost in manpower, time, and resources, and may lead to project abandonment.

questions.question: How should development stages be completed when building a usable extended reality system?
options: Quickly, so that the design-prototype-evaluate loop can be repeated often
Repeatedly, so that coding can be tested many times
After empirical study, so that usability can be confirmed
Carefully, so that there is no need to return to previous stages
questions.explanation: The development stages should be completed carefully so that the need to return to previous stages does not arise.

questions.question: Which stages in the interactive system development lifecycle are named as the places where building interactive software differs from building regular software?
options: Requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study
Coding, implementation, and code testing
Requirement gathering, coding and code testing, and empirical study
Feasibility study, analysis, and specification
questions.explanation: The stated differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

questions.question: How does the interactive system development lifecycle describe the relationship between interactive software development and regular software development?
options: They are identical at every development stage
They are entirely separate development processes
They are broadly similar, with differences in selected stages
They differ mainly in coding, implementation, and code testing
questions.explanation: Building interactive software is described as broadly similar to building regular software, with the differences occurring in particular stages.

Early evaluation

questions.question: Why does building usable XR software as interactive software for laypersons require a highly iterative software development lifecycle, and what role do iterations play?
questions.reference_answer: User-centered design involves users in the overall design lifecycle to produce usable application software, and the XR application software being developed is interactive software for laypersons. A highly iterative lifecycle is required because users' needs and expectations change the stage sequence and create loops in which a developer can return to a previous stage. Iterations between stages account for user feedback, which means involving users in different ways rather than only through feedback.

questions.question: Why is the design-prototype-evaluate loop expected to be performed quickly and repeatedly, while loops involving code design, coding, code testing, or empirical study should not be frequent?
questions.reference_answer: The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines early designs by prototyping a design, evaluating it to identify problems, and refining it through many iterations until few significantly different problems remain. Its stages must be completed quickly so that many iterations can occur within a reasonable time, because otherwise turnaround time increases significantly. Other loops, such as the loop between code design, coding, and code testing and the loop between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and coding, implementation, and empirical studies, should not be frequent because they significantly affect the project's overall outcome and turnaround time, escalate development cost in manpower, time, and resources, and may lead to project abandonment.

questions.question: Why is an empirical study needed in interactive system development even when code testing shows that the code executes properly?
questions.reference_answer: Code testing tests executability by ensuring that the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish whether the system is usable from the end user's point of view. The empirical study is a usability-testing stage that uses systematic testing with end users to ensure that the interactive system product conforms to usability. This stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development, in which end users are not involved.

questions.question: Why must requirement gathering in an interactive-system development lifecycle involve end users as well as the client, and what methods can be used for this stage?
questions.reference_answer: In interactive system development, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the client, while typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client. Methods for gathering end-user requirements include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes. Requirement gathering is one stage in which building interactive software differs from building regular software.
